About a year ago, I made the jump in full-force and opted to build myself a PC for gaming, but also double it as a bit of a workstation for most of my most of my internet use, work, etc. I'm fully satisfied with how it's gone, glad I built it, no regrets doing so, etc, etc. However, a lot of people that I know play on PS4, and I sometimes miss the social side a little bit, as I used to play regularly with friends on my PS3. I'd say I'm mostly a pretty single-player-game guy by default, but I do miss the firing up a game, picking up a controller, and having a fun time with friends. I do play with friends on PC, but a fair chunk I know instead opted for a PS4 or also own one in addition to a PC.

The main reasons for me thinking of getting one are;

- Most multiplatform stuff I'll probably play on PC, but exclusives like Uncharted 4 and Ratchet and Clank are releasing (and I thoroughly enjoyed playing Uncharted on PS3), plus shooters like Battlefield that friends play have a decent player base in terms of numbers (I remember reading something about *Battlefront* having the most players on PS4, in comparison to Xbox One and PC when put together iirc). They also regularly plaster how many million units it's shipped (partly as a middle finger to Microsoft), but the playerbase is clearly there.

- PC occasionally misses out (for example, the whole PT stuff) and having to wait for things; for example, MGSV's multiplayer mode arrived on PC in January, whereas consoles got it in the October, and GTA V got re-released for PS4/Xbox One just over a year after the 2013 release, whereas it arrived on PC an extra 5 months after the re-released versions.

- Certain games are easier (or more suited) to play with a controller, and make for comfier gaming. I play *Rocket League* fairly regularly on my PC with a controller. However, Rocket League was one of the free titles for those who have a PS Plus subscription, whereas I had to buy it, so I see benefits to playing on a PS4, especially where a controller may be concerned (as RL is very much more suited to a controller).

- I also saw recently of an update that allowed better compatibility with custom hard drives, which makes the initial purchase cheaper, as I could pick up the (new model) 500GB system and upgrade with my own hard drives, instead of spending the extra on the 1TB system. I could even pick one up pre-owned to cut costs further, as well as scoring some games with it (as people put up bundles on places such as eBay).

- I purchased some recording gear to record gameplay with my PS3/PC. However, my PC is now far more powerful, and could suffice for streaming PS4 gameplay. 'm not super big into streaming/gameplay, but it's at least something I can further explore with a PS4.

- I never really did it, but I have a lot of PS3 games lying around as I was never really fond of the idea of trade-ins, but at the end of the day, there is a physical product I could sell on if I so chose. Digital games on PC aren't great in the regard.

- Slightly off-topic but still relevant; my birthday will be coming up shortly and I don't see the harm in treating myself to one, you know, just for the hell of it.

However, the downsides that I see are;

- it costs to play online (there are free games as pat of PS Plus, but it's not like they're particularly standout titles).

- The price for one still seems relatively high, considering it's been out for over 2 years.

- Potential risk of essentially purchasing an expensive paperweight, although I could easily sell and recoup the funds if I was severely disappointed.

So I suppose I'm trying to gather s'more reasons for purchasing one. I will ultimately decide for myself, but I was curious if there are any obvious reasons I'm missing, any drawbacks or things you don't like from an owner's point of view, or anything else to add, just to like help me make a more informed decision.

I'm going to be busy this afternoon but I'll probably check back in a few hours and maybe add a few more reasons etc.

When working with food, there are various indicators of how long food is edible and how long it can be stored before bacterial and fungal growth begin. The browning process is a very important part of this timeline. It tell us exactly how long the produce has been exposed to the air ( and microbes) and how long it will be safe to eat before potentially unsafe levels of microbial growth set in. In the US, many of these timelines are enshrined in food safety laws with differing guidelines for vegetables and fruits stored whole or cut. He lashed vast numbers of triremes and fifty-oared galleys together, bows-on to the current: 360 for the bridge nearest the Black Sea, laid north-east from Nagara Point, and some 4,220 yards in length; 314 for that towards Maidos, across the narrows, which measured a little over two miles. Both positions had excellent landing-points. Each boat was held in place by two specially-designed anchors, strong enough to withstand gales from either the Black Sea or the Aegean. Across these boats, from shore to shore, were laid huge cables, two of flax and four of papyrus to each bridge, the former weighing about two hundredweight a fathom.

When they were secured at all points, Harpalus had them winched taut with huge wooden windlasses. The structure at this point somewhat resembled a railway line laid on its sleepers. Planks were then cut to match the floats, and cross-tied, close-lapping, over the cables. This surface was first covered with a layer of brushwood, and finally hard-packed with earth.

Last of all, a parapet was built along either side, to prevent animals falling off, or panicking at the sight of the water below them. At three points on each bridge the pontoons could be floated to allow merchantmen passage under the cables: presumably this involved unstepping their masts.
